item.title: Student Protests Mushroom Across Europe, Exposing Bleak Views of the Future
item.description:
Young Spaniards and Portuguese have pitched tents in their countries’ capitals to protest high rents. French and Italian students have marched en masse for better school conditions in demonstrations marred by looters.

Greeks protested for more university funding and young Albanians clashed with the police after joining broad anti-corruption demonstrations against a government they accused of impeding their prospects.

These are among the young Europeans who have taken to the streets in recent days in at least eight countries across the continent. Their demands vary according to the context and the government, but a common thread unites them all: They fear for their future.

“The no-future generation is back,” Sacha Cossi, 27, a concert stagehand, said on Tuesday as he sat with a group of other young Spaniards under a low tarp in the tent encampment in central Madrid.

Mr. Cossi said the tent city, there for weeks, reflected a continent-wide exasperation over low salaries and high rents, an impotence in the face of global warming and a general anxiety about job prospects and the potential disappearance of the generous welfare benefits enjoyed by previous generations.

“We are tired of everything,” he said, adding: “Things keep changing in a way that doesn’t benefit us.”

The protesters’ gloom reflects a continent that is struggling to find a way forward. Europe’s populations are aging, its debt is rising as governments struggle with growing expenses for pensions and other programs, and governments are reluctant to raise taxes. Immigration is polarizing electorates.

There is widespread fear that Europe is failing to keep pace with the technological upheavals that are expected to define the near future, and it is caught in the middle of a contest between the world’s two great powers, America and China. Things seem less secure in the face of spreading Russian aggression, as President Trump, who threatened to attack the territory of a European ally, Denmark, withdraws support for Ukraine.

The malaise affects Europeans of all ages, but it is the continent’s young who face the bleakest long-term landscape. The public services and benefits that defined European society for decades are becoming increasingly unsustainable, with governments struggling to pay for pensions for the old, schools for the young, and housing, transportation and health care needed by everyone. Military spending, which has increased as the United States reduces its defense commitment, has added extra stress on budgets.

Governments of all ideological stripes — a right-wing leader in Italy, a left-wing one in Spain, a moderate in France — are all struggling to provide a plausible answer. Europe’s young increasingly feel left out of the picture.

“There’s this sense of rejection, fatigue,” said Stella Salis, 22, a protester and university student in Padua.

In terms of protester numbers and longevity, the movements are still not near the scale of the anti-austerity protests that spread across the world in the years that followed the 2008 financial crisis.

But they are beginning to catch the world’s attention and spur talk among protesters of a transnational movement. French high school students helped energize teenage counterparts in Belgium, while protesters in Italy and Germany have begun using a slogan that originated in France.

Ms. Salis said that she hoped that the protest movement was “starting to be in a phase that transcends national borders.”

Yet in some countries, the unrest has emboldened the far right as much as it has galvanized the left, often overshadowing the protesters’ messages.

Rioting in northern Italy this past weekend led to dozens of arrests, and gave Matteo Salvini, a government minister and hard-right leader, the pretext to announce that the government would dispatch 500 soldiers to “defend Milan,” from “criminals.” With his party slipping in the polls, Mr. Salvini seized on the unrest to promote his anti-immigration agenda, saying he hoped the rioting ended, “once and for all,” leftist calls to extend citizenship to children of immigrants before they reach the age of 18.

In France, the far-right National Rally has had a field day presenting itself as the party best able to prevent a repeat of the lawlessness perpetrated in French cities this past weekend.

“In six months, the French people will be able to choose a different path: That of restored authority and security,” Marine Le Pen, the party’s candidate in the presidential election next spring, said in a speech on Sunday.

It was a message echoed that same day by her party president, Jordan Bardella. “We stand ready to restore order in the country,” Mr. Bardella said after emerging from a police station located near the epicenter of recent unrest.

Yet whoever takes power across Europe in the coming months will have few easy offerings for young people. They will face excruciating decisions about what public services to fund with declining resources in an environment marked by economic headwinds, including inflation, rising bond yields and soaring fuel prices.

“My dream would be to have a job that I love,” said Salomé Regnaud, a 15-year-old student who has been protesting for better school conditions in France. “Not to have to look at my expenses every month and ask myself, ‘Will I be able to do this?’ or ‘Can I afford to buy that?’”

It was a lament that had echoes from Portugal in the west to Albania in the east.

“People say we don’t want to work? We do want to work, but with dignified conditions,” said Mourana Monteiro, 29, a psychologist in Lisbon who on Tuesday night joined a few thousand Portuguese to protest real estate speculation that has contributed to rising housing costs.

She had been staying in a tent encampment since Saturday and looked forward to a teacher’s strike the following week. “What’s the point of working and then not being able to afford a house, pay our bills at the end of the month, have a family?” Ms. Monteiro asked.

In Albania, students have joined a broader anti-government “Flamingo” movement. It is named for the bird habitat in an area where Jared Kushner, Mr. Trump’s son-in-law, won government approval for a major luxury tourism development that is opposed by environmental groups.

Albanians in the anti-corruption movement are calling for the ouster of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has in turn called them radical leftists, but the students have focused on protections for education.

“We are a generation that has chosen not to remain silent, unlike our parents, who did not enjoy the same freedoms or the full right to freedom of expression,” said Redjan Shkëmbi, a 22-year-old actor, referring to the dictatorship that ruled the country until 1991.

Mr. Shkëmbi joined the first protests in Zvernec nearly 150 days ago to call for more funding for the education system and public hospitals, and said his main motivation was to fight for a more transparent and democratic Albania.

“We want a better country,” he said, “and we want to contribute to its future.”

Reporting was contributed by Ségolène Le Stradic from Paris; Josephine de La Bruyère from Rome; Carlos Barragán from Madrid; Daniela Ferreira Pinto from Lisbon; and Fatjona Mejdini from Tirana, Albania.

item.title: A Debt-Fueled “Doom Loop”
item.description:
When government debt gets out of hand, it’s a problem. In the run-up to the French Revolution, the French monarchy was heavily indebted and losing the ability to borrow from international bankers. Then the price of bread spiked, and the rest, as they say, is history.

What’s happening in France today is not a revolution. But the combination of weak government finances, investors worried about getting repaid and angry citizens is as explosive as ever — not just in France, but in many countries. Today my colleagues Eshe Nelson and Jim Tankersley write about something called the populism-bond market “doom loop.” Read on.

By Eshe Nelson and Jim Tankersley

When protests over high gas prices ripped through France in 2018, President Emmanuel Macron offered about $11 billion in tax cuts and wage increases to try to quell the unrest.

He can’t do that this time around.

Today, protests that initially began over education have turned violent. But Macron is no longer in a position to throw money at the problem.

That’s because the French government is also fighting the prospect of a crisis in its bond market. Investors have been dumping French debt, unsure of the government’s ability to manage its budget amid high interest rates and political uncertainty; announcing a big financial commitment to mollify protesters would most likely only rattle investors further.

Macron, in other words, is in a tight spot. Do nothing, and the protests could continue. Spend more, and he could ultimately leave France with even less money for areas like education, by making borrowing even more expensive. Both scenarios would most likely add to the momentum of the populist politicians running for his seat next year.

Trapped between angry citizens, and wary investors, Macron could wind up in an unhappy place — what researchers described to us as a populism-bond market “doom loop.”

Voters vs. investors

France is not the only country facing a debt trap. As borrowing has grown in many wealthy nations, including France, Britain and the United States, populist politics are surging. The combination makes for a combustible mix.

Market turmoil and political tumult can feed off each other, according to Michal Brzozowski and Joanna Siwinska-Gorzelak, researchers at the University of Warsaw in Poland, who published a paper on the relationship between populism and fiscal policy.

At the root of the problem is a considerable tension: Amid deep political and fiscal uncertainty, voters and investors appear to want different things.

Buyers of debt want to be adequately compensated for the risk of lending to governments. When they see governments unable to make difficult choices, such as cutting spending or increasing taxes, to reduce yawning budget deficits, what they see is a loan that’s getting riskier. As a result, they demand higher interest payments.

Voters, though, are increasingly turning to populist parties that largely reject the idea that budgets require these difficult choices. Instead, they promise to protect generous retirement programs and other spending, while often proposing to cut taxes, or to raise taxes only on the wealthy, which in most cases wouldn’t go far enough.

The resulting tensions could spiral like this: Economically anxious voters turn to populists, who promise a pain-free return to better days, and buyers of government debt recoil.

Catch-22

Some centrist politicians today are still pledging fiscal discipline — the kind of pledges that voters once rewarded. But today, such policies tend to leave the public with the impression that those politicians are largely powerless to improve conditions, said Ludovic Subran, the chief investment officer and chief economist at Allianz, the German insurance company.

“That’s really the Catch-22 of politics today,” Subran said. The politicians who have felt the disciplinary hand of the market are punished politically, while more populist parties “say whatever they want to say.”

Eventually these problems will come to a head, said Simon Radford, the director for policy and programming for the Milken Institute in Europe.

“If you’re not going to solve it with new growth, and if interest payments are outrunning growth, then eventually what can’t go on forever, won’t go on forever,” he said. Too much borrowing, and too little economic growth will eventually become unsustainable, regardless of who’s in power and what they say while they’re campaigning.

Though Marine Le Pen, the far-right front-runner in France’s presidential election, has vowed to reduce the deficit, economists question the credibility of her financial plan, which would lower the retirement age while slashing spending on state bodies and cutting the country’s contribution to the European Union. All those measures would be difficult to enact. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, France’s far-left candidate, has alarmed investors by proposing to effectively cancel some of the country’s debt instead of repaying it.

At this point, it’s looking increasingly possible that these two candidates could be facing off against one another in next year’s presidential elections. Investors are already grimacing.

Russia yesterday released a 74-year-old American teacher, Stephen James Hubbard, who had been held for four years after being convicted of being a Ukrainian mercenary. President Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, praised President Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian” for the move, which was not part of a prisoner swap.

Why did Putin agree to Hubbard’s release? He probably concluded it would be strategically favorable to him to make this gesture to Trump at a time when he is “winning the American president to Russia’s side,” David Sanger, our White House and national security correspondent, said. Watch him explain in the video above.

Trump’s approval rating hit a new low less than two weeks before the midterm elections.

Elon Musk said that SpaceX and Tesla were exploring a merger to create a single company worth more than $3 trillion.

A U.S. judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion for deceiving Facebook users about its data privacy practices.

China is proposing rules that could give its government new powers to track, and potentially limit, where its A.I. systems are used.

The Tata Group, India’s biggest company, is 158 years old and employs over a million people. Now the founding family is fighting its celebrated chairman for control.

Ten public housing towers collapsed within seconds during earthquakes in Venezuela in June. A Times investigation found fundamental flaws in their design and construction. Our reporter Julie Turkewitz explains in the video below.

A shark that became a celebrity in South Korea returned to the open ocean after being trapped in a canal for more than a month.

The most clicked link in your newsletter yesterday was about the search for the perfect dog.

Catherine Breed, an endurance athlete, became the first person ever to swim the entire California coastline. The journey took over 100 days and covered more than 1,000 kilometers as Breed braved storms, unpredictable currents and the fastest sharks in the ocean.

Videos made with A.I. are flooding Brazil’s internet ahead of a high-stakes presidential runoff on Sunday. The deluge is testing the country’s capacity to preserve the integrity of its elections.

Brazil bars candidates from using “deepfakes” while campaigning. It also requires campaigns to label videos generated by A.I. In practice, though, curbing the spread of A.I. falsehoods has been difficult. A.I. has emerged as a potent tool for spreading political misinformation — and even just for plain amusement. Take a look.

Dark nutrition isn’t a specific diet; it’s a way of thinking about food and health. It stems from a central principle: Most of what you think you know about food is wrong. What if broccoli is toxic? What if red meat and butter are actually healthy? What if roadkill is good for you?

A typical dark-nutrition meal might consist of raw beef liver, raw egg yolks and bee pollen. “People think my diet is extreme,” said one proponent. “But they’re eating processed food and drinking alcohol and basically poisoning themselves.”

Read: K-Ming Chang’s “Needlemouth” tells the story of three cousins grappling with their inherited trauma.

Elevate: These simple tweaks can make your red sauce even more shirt-splatteringly delicious.

That’s it for today. See you tomorrow! — Katrin

Eshe Nelson and Jim Tankersley were our guest writers today.

item.title: Quebec Publisher Cuts Ties With Author Accused of Using A.I.
item.description:
A prestigious Quebec publisher said on Wednesday that it was cutting ties with an author after discovering he used artificial intelligence to help write a breakout novel.

The publisher, Les Éditions du Boréal, said it would not reprint “It Was Either That or Die,” or any other books by the author, Thélyson Orélien, after finding evidence of A.I. use in early versions of the manuscript.

Mr. Orélien, a Haitian-Canadian writer, is at the center of a literary scandal that has rocked France and prompted deep soul-searching about what the emergence of A.I. means for the future of writing.

The furor erupted last month after social media accounts, including one partially run by a columnist at a conservative newspaper, said that detection tools flagged “It Was Either That or Die” as partially written using A.I. The ensuing controversy led the Goncourt Academy — the institution overseeing France’s highest literary award — to pull the novel from its shortlist.

Grasset, the separate company that published Mr. Orélien’s book in France, did not respond to a request for comment. In a statement last week, Mr. Orélien said that “not a single sentence of this book was created by a machine, nor was the meaning or structure.” He conceded that “research tools” had been used, “particularly regarding foreign idioms,” without specifying further.

Mr. Orélien eventually admitted, however, that he had plagiarized opinion articles and a short story he published more than a decade ago.

Last month, Radio-Canada, a national public radio station, said that Mr. Orélien had plagiarized four opinion articles published in 2012 and 2013 on French and Canadian news sites, as well as sections of the award-winning 2012 short story.

As accusations flew last month, Les Éditions du Boréal initially said it could neither confirm nor rule out Mr. Orélien’s use of A.I. and cautioned against drawing “hasty conclusions.” The publisher said that it would suspend promotional activities out of concern for the author and that it was helping him compile a dossier of early drafts.

On Wednesday, the publisher said it had ordered an external analysis of the book after Mr. Orélien stopped cooperating with its investigation. “The results received this week revealed traces of A.I. tags in the metadata of certain documents,” its statement said.

“We still do not know to what extent A.I. was used in the creation” of the book, the publisher said, “and we will likely never have a definitive answer.” But it said, “for us, the fundamental issue is one of trust between authors and publishers.”

Les Éditions du Boréal nevertheless called for an end to personal attacks against Mr. Orélien. In his statement last week, Mr. Orélien, who is Black, said that while criticism was always legitimate, the “threats,” “media lynching” and “racist harassment” to which he had been subjected over the preceding weeks had been “unbearable.”

The publisher’s announcement came the day after submissions opened for the “Prix Pascal,” a competition for French-language manuscripts “co-written” with A.I., according to the prize’s website.

Ségolène Le Stradic contributed reporting.

item.title: Pope Needs No Further Treatment for Lung Cancer, Doctors Say
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV will need no further treatment after his surgery for lung cancer, his doctors announced on Wednesday.

The pope’s personal doctor and the surgeon who removed a lower lobe of the pope’s right lung at Gemelli Hospital in Rome on Oct. 13 said in a statement that follow-up tests confirmed that the cancer was localized.

“A subsequent oncology evaluation confirmed that no further treatment is necessary,” the doctors wrote.

The announcement came eight days after the pontiff’s diagnosis was revealed publicly, casting his agenda into uncertainty some 18 months into his papacy.

On Sunday, at his first public event since being discharged from the hospital a day earlier, Leo told the faithful gathered for his weekly prayer and blessing in St. Peter’s Square that he would “gradually” return to work.

That included wading into international politics, speaking by phone over the weekend with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia to call for a cease-fire in the war so that civilians could evacuate from a besieged city in Ukraine. Two days later, he spoke with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine about a cease-fire.

This week, Leo met with participants at a conference at the Vatican. He appointed 24 members to a theological commission, doubling the number of lay people and increasing the number of women to eight from five.

On Wednesday, the pope reappeared in St. Peter’s Square for his weekly audience. He kicked off the event by riding through a cheering crowd on the so-called pope mobile, waving and stopping to bless babies.

Leo’s first major health scare as pontiff began less than two weeks ago, when he told a crowd gathered in St. Peter’s Square for Sunday prayer that he would have a small growth on his lung removed. Two days later, the surgery was performed and doctors confirmed that he had lung adenocarcinoma, as preoperative tests had shown. Information later released by the Vatican suggested the cancer had been caught at an early stage.

In their statement on Wednesday evening, the doctors said that test results on the tissue removed during the surgery “confirmed that the tumor was a lung adenocarcinoma and that the disease was localized.”

Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer. Doctors can treat that cancer with surgery alone when it is caught early. A patient may simply need frequent monitoring. Advances in treatment, including immunotherapies and drugs that target specific mutations, have helped reduce the likelihood of recurrence and improved the prognosis for later-stage lung cancers.

In an interview with Vatican News, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, the thoracic surgeon who operated on Pope Leo, said the operation had been routine “in the sense that, in similar cases involving a lung tumor of a certain size, the entire lobe containing it has to be removed.”

He added that he was pleased with the pope’s postoperative recovery. “The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery, as the most motivated people do after this kind of operation,” Dr. Margaritora said.

The pope is scheduled to travel to South America on Nov. 6 for an 11-day trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. After Leo’s operation, concerns were raised about the schedule, which includes many flights and some high-altitude stops in Peru. The pope has made clear that he is still hoping to travel.

Nina Agrawal contributed reporting.

item.title: Bukele Issues Harsh Warning to Haitian Gangs
item.description:
President Nayib Bukele of El Salvador issued a sharply worded warning to Haitian gang members who kidnapped four of his countrymen this week: We are coming for you.

Mr. Bukele said a military operation had been launched to rescue four missing Salvadoran aviation technicians who were abducted in a gang stronghold outside the capital on Sunday. Mr. Bukele was in discussions to send more troops to conduct operations and assist in the rescue attempt, according to a person familiar with the episode who was not authorized to discuss the matter publicly.

The four missing Salvadorans are members of a new United Nations-backed military force called the Gang Suppression Force, which is aimed at wresting control of Haiti from gangs that hold much of its capital.

The four Salvadorans were ambushed Sunday afternoon in a gang attack while driving back to their base from a supermarket in the town of Croix-des-Bouquets. Their armored S.U.V. was hit by explosives and caught fire, but the four soldiers escaped, the Salvadoran military said.

Nobody has heard from them since.

In a social media message written in Creole and directed at gang leaders, Mr. Bukele stressed that the four missing men were not combatants. El Salvador’s contingent in the Gang Suppression Force is made up of pilots and technical personnel whose primary job is to carry out medical evacuations and save lives, “not to wage war,” Mr. Bukele said.

Mr. Bukele, a right-wing leader in office since 2019, is widely known for overseeing a harsh crackdown on El Salvador’s gangs. A nation once awash in violence is now among the safest in the world. And with thousands of accused gang members locked up in a maximum-security prison, it has the highest incarceration rate in the world.

His post included a video clip of armored military vehicles firing weapons in a desolate street that appeared to have been the scene of heavy fighting.

A military operation launched to rescue the missing Salvadorans has a single mission to bring them back alive, he said.

“I want you, the gang leaders, to understand one thing very clearly: today’s attack is nothing compared to what is coming if we do not get all four hostages back alive,” he wrote. “And do not take our word for empty threats. We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too.”

But he said gang members still have time to avoid repercussions.

“Return our four compatriots to us alive, without any harm, and everything will go back to how it was before the kidnapping,” he wrote. “The decision is in your hands.”

The Gang Suppression Force and a Haitian National Police task force comprised largely of private military contractors who launch drone strikes have been engaged in battle with gang members in the area where the abduction took place for days.

Several gang members were killed and four Gang Suppression Force soldiers were injured in operations to try to find the men, the force said in a statement.

Initial reports indicating that five Salvadorans had gone missing were incorrect, the Gang Suppression Force said.

The Gang Suppression Force arrived in Haiti in April with the mission to aggressively go after gangs wreaking havoc in the country.

More than 22,000 people have died in gang violence and police operations in the past five years as Haiti battles armed groups that terrorize entire communities.

Authorized by the U.N. Security Council, the force was expected to reach 5,500 troops, but has struggled to achieve full capacity. It currently comprises about 2,000 soldiers from six countries: Guatemala, Jamaica, Chad, El Salvador, Mongolia and Sri Lanka.

“Gangs are testing the G.S.F.,” the force’s special representative, Jack Christofides, told the U.N. Security Council on Monday. “We recorded an increase in hostile incidents against our force — from two to 15 in a single month.”

Haitian government officials did not respond to requests for comment.

On Wednesday, three days after the kidnapping, Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé released a statement calling the abduction “an absolute priority” for state authorities.

Emiliano Rodríguez Mega contributed reporting.

item.title: Australian Zoo Plays Matchmaker for Giant Birds, and Big Green Eggs Are Proof
item.description:
There was no guarantee Martina and Jeffrey, southern cassowary birds living at an Australian zoo, would hit it off.

Staff members and visitors at the Adelaide Zoo are marveling at the vivid proof of the successful breeding: Martina recently laid two fluorescent green eggs.

It’s the first cassowary egg at the zoo in 34 years. There have been fewer than 10 chicks in the last 10 years at Australia’s other zoos.

The birds, known as the most dangerous in the world, are a protected species. Just about 4,500 southern cassowaries remain in the wild in Australia, with their habitat under threat. Breeding them in a zoo requires a carefully managed conservation plan, which includes approval by a zoo association and observing the birds’ behavior.

Complicating matters is that they’re solitary creatures.

Chad Crittle, the director of the Adelaide Zoo, likened the effort to breed Martina and Jeffrey to online dating, “where it might look like everything lines up really well. We like the same things and you might like the same food, but when you actually meet, it doesn’t always work and the same can be for animals in a zoo setting as part of these programs.”

The birds, which are the heaviest in Australia, “can be dangerous if you put yourself in their space,” Mr. Crittle said, describing a large claw on its toe that the birds kick with. Martina’s last weigh-in: 166 pounds.

When handlers introduced them in September, Mr. Crittle said, “Jeffrey moved into action within about two minutes of meeting Martina.”

The first egg appeared last week, and the second followed on Monday. Martina, 10, could lay a third egg on Thursday.

Mr. Crittle compared the egg’s hue to a lime-green highlighter. The color is meant to protect the eggs in the rainforest, he said.

It’s not clear if any of the eggs are viable, but Mr. Crittle is excited about the eggs because of the tricky effort to breed the birds.

Once Martina is done laying eggs, it will be Jeffrey’s job to incubate them and rear any chicks. Incubation time is about 50 days, the zoo said.

Zoo staff members could try to take blood from the eggs to determine viability. “But our preference at the moment is to be hands-off and let him have his first go at doing this so he can learn,” Mr. Crittle said.

Visitors to the southern Australia zoo can get a good look at the neon eggs because Martina “decided to lay the eggs right next to the front of her habitat,” Mr. Crittle said. “Once he starts to sit, you won’t then be able to see the eggs until, fingers crossed, they hatch.”

item.title: ‘Open War’ Between Afghanistan and Pakistan Adds a Volatile Element
item.description:
China has tried to mediate, unsuccessfully. So have Russia, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Qatar. And yet the conflict between Pakistan and Afghanistan shows no sign of ending, and each side appears to have abandoned diplomacy. Proxy groups are also playing a growing role in the fighting.

In the latest round of fighting on Saturday, Pakistan’s military claims to have destroyed a military camp along the rugged, porous border and killed Afghan soldiers. A provincial spokesman for the Afghan military denied that there were any Afghan casualties and claimed instead that the Taliban had killed 13 Pakistani soldiers.

The conflict could become even more unpredictable, said Ibraheem Bahiss, an expert on Afghanistan at the International Crisis Group, as both sides embrace proxy groups: The Taliban in Afghanistan are accused of failing to restrain incursions by armed groups in the borderland that target Pakistan, while Pakistan is warming to the idea of supporting anti-Taliban armed opposition.

On Sept. 27, the Taliban said they had killed 28 militiamen and captured 32 others who had tried to enter Afghanistan from Pakistan. The Pakistani government called the accusations “baseless.”

“The proxy standoff is intensifying, and that’s a more dangerous escalation,” Mr. Bahiss said.

Pakistan’s military and intelligence officials have met with leaders of anti-Taliban armed groups in recent months to offer potential support, according to a Pakistani intelligence official, a former national security official briefed on the meetings, and a senior Afghan member of one of those groups.

The conflict between the two countries, which escalated when Pakistan declared “open war” in late February, has stymied months of effort to broker peace and killed or injured at least 1,100 Afghan civilians. More than 730 civilians have been killed in militant attacks in Pakistan this year, according to the South Asia Terrorism Portal, a New Delhi-based monitoring platform.

In April, China hosted talks that went nowhere. On Oct. 5, a meeting in Moscow on Afghan security among 10 countries in the region failed to produce a joint statement because of disagreements between the Afghan and Pakistani delegations, according to Vladimir V. Putin’s special representative for Russia.

“The two sides are so fixated on their own position and righteousness of their arguments that no one has the ability to coerce or strong-arm either, even China,” said Mr. Bahiss.

“It is progressing from a low-grade confrontation to an entrenched conflict that has the potential to spiral out of control,” said Amira Jadoon, an associate professor of political science at Clemson University and a South Asia security expert. “But the underlying issue is never resolved.”

That issue is the Taliban’s support for the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, also known as the Pakistani Taliban. Thousands of militants from the group navigate the porous border to stage attacks on Pakistani security forces. Security experts and officials attribute a sharp increase in attacks on Pakistan to the permissive environment provided by the Afghan Taliban since 2021.

There have been, on average, more than one militant attack a day on Pakistani security forces this year, according to a tally by the Pak Institute of Peace Studies, a research center based in Islamabad, the Pakistani capital.

The Taliban have denied providing any support for militant attacks on Pakistan.

Publicly, both sides say they remain open to diplomacy, but the Pakistani government says it won’t negotiate with the Taliban until they commit to stopping supporting militant groups.

Until then, Pakistani military and political leaders view military action as the only option left, according to Aarish Khan, an analyst at a government-funded research center in Islamabad, even though that may push the Taliban to rely even further on the militants attacking Pakistan.

“It doesn’t seem to be as much a long-term strategy as the outcome of pent-up frustration,” said Mr. Khan, head of the Afghanistan program at the Institute of Regional Studies. “And pent-up frustration isn’t viable in the long term.”

Civilians on both sides of the border say they are bearing the brunt of the violence.

In the Pakistani province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, some residents said they worry that a recent power grab by the federal government against provincial officials could give the military an even freer hand in launching operations without any accountability.

“It will cause displacement again and create more chaos,” said Amjad Wazir, a university student from the region.

Across the border, Mohammad Idris Zazi, a taxi driver in Paktia Province, where Saturday’s clashes erupted, said he could not work because of the relentless airstrikes and shelling. He said, “What have we done wrong to deserve to become victims of disputes between the two countries?”

Zia ur-Rehman and Safiullah Padshah contributed reporting.

item.title: Archers Mount Their Steeds in Pursuit of Centuries-Old Warrior Spirit
item.description:
The sun was behind me as I approached the target quickly. My horse was in a slow run, and I stood up, knees braced against the saddle and heels down in the stirrups, trying to stay steady even though I felt as if I were in a wind tunnel.

Moving swiftly, I drew an arrow from my quiver and loaded the bow, pulled my arm back and released. There were no foes nor frontline. Rather, I was engaging in the pastime of horseback archery.

There’s something oddly comforting about playing at ancient warfare, about reliving the days when empires spread and fell on the tip of an arrow, especially nowadays when high-tech conflict rages around us.

Horseback archery is experiencing a renaissance across Asia, the Middle East and even Europe as real war becomes ever more destructive and impersonal, fought with drones and artificial intelligence. The allure of what is also called mounted archery always makes me think of the romanticization of Civil War re-enactors, but for an even more bygone era.

Last month, amid the lush mountains of Kyrgyzstan where the Mongol Empire once marched westward on the strength of its mounted archers, it indeed looked like several period dramas had come to life. Athletes participating in the World Nomad Games, an international tournament rooted in ancient warfare and ethnosports, were clad in warrior wear and demonstrating battlefield skills that once could earn someone acclaim.

For months, I had been training in my spare time for the tournament. I had no previous experience riding or doing archery until I came to the sport about two years ago as I was in the midst of reporting as a foreign correspondent on Israel’s retaliatory war against Hamas in Gaza, leaving the Palestinian territory devastated.

While it may seem odd to enjoy an archaic form of warfare while covering a brutal present-day conflict, there was a meditative aspect to the activity, requiring complete concentration, graceful technique and matching your breath to your movements; it blocked out the modern world, even if only for a few seconds.

I had hoped to compete and was set to join the team from Jordan, because I live there as a Amman-based correspondent. But even a tournament celebrating the nomadic way of life still respects the borders of modern nation-states, and because I am not a Jordanian citizen, I was ineligible to compete with the team. Instead, I joined it as a coach.

The Nomad Games began in 2014 and has grown steadily. This year, its sixth, had hundreds of athletes from more than 100 countries competing in various ethnosports such as powerlifting camel-shaped weights, speed building circular tents known as yurts and the ever popular kok-boru, a version of polo played with a headless goat carcass instead of a ball.

Horseback archery itself began its comeback about 15 years ago, drawing in people who are interested in history and others who simply like the athletic challenge of it.

“For sure we think about how our ancestors used to wage war and this was a big part of it,” Abdulrahman Algharaibeh said one day during practice, dressed in lace-up boots, cargo pants, a camo shirt and a baseball cap that made him look more like a U.S. military contractor than a Jordanian Bedouin warrior. “That stays rooted in our mind for sure.”

He recalled watching a popular Turkish drama, Resurrection: Ertugrul — about a 13th-century Turkic chieftain battling the Crusaders, Byzantines and Mongols — and a specific scene in which the protagonists launched an attack on horseback.

“I got very excited,” said Mr. Algharaibeh, a 30-year-old software engineer. “I wanted a horse right away so I could do like them.”

Sitting on a hill at the Nomad Games overlooking the course, Mr. Algharaibeh, Mohammad Al-Khanazreh, another member of the Jordanian team and I watched the competition. Nearby, a man dressed like an ancient Mongolian warrior sat with a falcon in his lap.

Below us, athletes from other countries galloped along the 100-meter-long horseback archery course, finishing in under 14 seconds. The heavy drumbeat of hooves was interrupted only by the occasional thwap of an arrow hitting one of three targets.

“People are going back to their histories,” said Mr. Al-Khanazreh, 42, a retired security officer turned full-time equestrian and archery instructor. “A long time ago they would say that the true horseman is the one who has his sword, his lance, his bow and his shield,” he said, citing a common refrain attributed to the eras of Islamic conquest.

But even on the very first day of the men’s competition, we were pulled back to the present and reminded of modern warfare.

Overnight, Iran had fired missiles at an American military base in Jordan, among other regional targets, saying the strikes came in response to a U.S. attack on southern Iran, which hit a wedding and killed five guests. Mr. Algharaibeh had been hearing from friends and family in Jordan unsettled by the alerts on their phones warning of incoming attacks.

Earlier this year, our preparation for the tournament had also been impacted by the regional war, with Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz delaying a shipment of arrows, leaving our supply running low.

Even when properly armed, horseback archers face a challenge mastering the sport.

During practices, my coach, Bassam Al-Mhana, always urges me to focus, as if I could possibly do anything else when I shoot an arrow.

In a matter of seconds, I have to stand up in the saddle atop my running horse, my knees gripping it tight and heels pushed down in the stirrups to remain steady; smoothly draw an arrow from the quiver, and in one motion load it onto my bow ; and pull my right arm back and release the arrow before passing the target. All this while keeping my eyes on the target andensuring my horse’s gait remains fast and consistent.

One morning, as I was joined at a practice by a Jordanian man dressed like a Bedouin and a Lebanese man who was planning to open his own horseback archery school in Beirut, Mr. Al-Mhana urged us on. “Guys, it’s as if you are heading out to battle,” he shouted.

As the three of us trotted our horses to the start of the course, he added with a chuckle, “Don’t forget to share with us the spoils of war.”

But any spoils these days for mounted archers only take the form of the admiration of peers and the occasional tournament prize.

One competitor, Balazs Vermes, 36, dressed like a 10th-century Hungarian warrior, said he was trying to embody the warrior spirit of his ancestors.

Modern warfare has removed much of the human variable from the battlefield, he said. “Back then if you were good, you had the chance to survive,” he said. “Now you could be very good but in one second a drone can kill you.”

Despite the passage of the centuries, war remains unpredictable, as does the competition.

“I look at this as a battlefield,” Mr. Vermes said. “Things change and I need to adjust.”

By the time he took to the course, it was raining heavily with nearly everyone except the competitors huddled under tents. The rain had softened the track, making it even more challenging for those yet to compete, and the horses’ hooves sent clumps of mud flying into the air.

It was a reminder that in sport, as in war, not everyone competes on an even battlefield.

item.title: Protesters in Indonesia Demand Action to Stop Fires in Rainforests
item.description:
Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets this week in Indonesia to voice anger at what they see as their government’s failure to stop fires in rainforests that have blanketed their country in a sickening haze.

The demonstrations by students and members of civil society groups began on Monday and spread to more than a half dozen cities across the country including on the island of Borneo, where many of the fires are burning.

These are the latest in a series of protests that have been building since August, in which participants have demanded that the nation’s president, Prabowo Subianto, declare a national emergency and take steps to prevent destructive agricultural practices that many blame for fueling the blazes.

“I have the right to breathe,” read one banner at a rally in the Indonesian capital, Jakarta. “Extinguish the fires immediately!”

“The situation has reached a level that is completely, utterly abnormal,” said one protester, Naomi Artika, a law student at the University of Palangka Raya in Central Kalimantan, a province on Borneo.

Government leaders defended their response, which has not been able to halt the fires.

“We are all trying our best,” the state secretary, Prasetyo Hadi, said on Tuesday, according to local media. “We have deployed ground troops, aircraft and volunteers to put out the fires.”

While fires appear every year during the dry season that begins in April, this year’s are the worst on record. Earlier this year, there was less rain during the usually wet months that precede April, which experts blamed on both global warming and an El Niño climate shift.

The size of the fires remains contested. In its last tally made in July, the Indonesian government said about 780 square miles had burned this year — twice the land area of New York City. But Nusantara Atlas, an open-access platform that tracks deforestation globally, estimates the amount of forest destroyed is closer to 7,400 square miles.

The smoke has spread into neighboring Malaysia and Singapore, which have also reacted angrily, blaming Indonesia for not doing enough to contain the blazes.

Within Indonesia, the smoke from the burning rainforests has created a growing health crisis that has closed schools, caused widespread breathing disorders and forced many to stay indoors.

According to the Health Ministry, more than 306,309 residents of Indonesia’s seven provinces most heavily affected by the smoke have suffered acute respiratory illnesses over the last two months. Nearly half of those — 146,037 cases — were children under the age of 10, the ministry said on Sunday.

Some medical experts say the figures undercount the actual number of people falling sick.

“Lately, we’ve been seeing more scans showing signs of pneumonia, particularly among children and the elderly,” said Sigit Riatno, a radiologist in Kandangan, a town in South Kalimantan on Borneo. Of the roughly 60 chest X-rays he examines each day, about a third now show evidence of respiratory problems. “This situation is really worrying.”

One of those forced to stay indoors is Davankan Khalid Bhumi, a 2-year-old who has been unable to leave his home in Pontianak, the capital of West Kalimantan Province on Borneo, to meet playmates or swim. The haze outside is just too thick for little Khalid, who has been sensitive to smoke since infancy and needs a respiratory device called a nebulizer three times a week to help him sleep, said his mother, Era Oktafiansyah.

“It breaks my heart to hear his ‘ngiik ngiik’ breath and coughing,” said Ms. Era, 30, using a word that describes the wheezing sound her son makes.

Indonesia’s burning rainforests are often pointed to as a symptom of an ailing planet, an environmental disruption on par with the deforestation of the Amazon. The fires are widely blamed on “slash-and-burn” clearing of rainforest for agriculture to grow cash crops including palm oil and timber. The flames jump to nearby areas of peat, a type of wetland made up of decaying plant matter that extends deep beneath the forest floor but that has dried out.

Once ignited, the peat can smolder out of control for weeks or even months.

Mr. Prabowo has ordered additional resources to reinforce firefighting operations across the country, calling it “a top priority for us.” At the same time, he has resisted declaring the fires a natural disaster, which would compel his government to take more action.

“Ultimately, the only real solution is rain,” he said last week.

His government has pursued other policies, including energy self-sufficiency, that opponents say are having an adverse impact on the rainforests.

The president’s special envoy for climate and energy has proposed using 49,000 square miles of degraded forest as feedstock for biofuel production. He said the plan wouldn’t cut down old-growth forest, but critics say it will still damage the overall ecosystem, leaving it more vulnerable to fires.

This week’s protests were also held on the second anniversary of the presidency of Mr. Prabowo, whom the demonstrators criticized for what they saw as a lack of action. “If we burn, you burn with us!” one banner said in Jakarta.

Last month, Nafas Kalbar, a coalition of civil society groups in West Kalimantan, filed a class-action lawsuit accusing the government of negligence in its failure to stop the blazes or to take preventive measures against the El Niño, which was foreseeable.

“Clean air and clean water are fundamental human rights,” said Glorio Sanen, the coalition’s lawyer.

In Malaysia, a former health minister, Khairy Jamaluddin, urged his government to push Indonesia to take action. “When somebody else is choking you, you don’t allow them to continue to choke you,” he said in a podcast.

Singapore’s prime minister, Lawrence Wong, said his country would punish private companies blamed for the destructive agricultural practices that cause the fires.

Dr. Sigit, the radiologist, says the prolonged haze will have health impacts reaching beyond even the proliferation of breathing ailments that he has observed. Many may suffer from chronic respiratory problems that will impose a long-term burden on their lives as well as on hospitals and Indonesia’s national health insurance program, whose budget is already strained.

“The impact of smog on health, especially the respiratory tract and lungs, will incur even greater costs,” he said.

Ms. Era, the mother of Khalid, looks forward to a day when the air is clean enough to allow her son to play outside again. In the meantime, she has closed gaps and openings around their home to stop the smoke from entering.

“We do stay indoors, but how do you keep a child from breathing?” she said.

item.title: Modi Seeks to Calm Allies by Shackling Gen Z Protests
item.description:
The ongoing youth protests rocking India caught Prime Minister Narendra Modi by surprise when they first broke out in the summer.

His deployment of police batons and tear gas, plus social media videos seeking to connect with Gen Z in their style, did little to contain them. A rare political climb-down, by sacrificing his education minister, got the protesters to go home for the time being, but it also emboldened his opponents.

So when the protesters announced another demonstration in the capital earlier this month, this time angry over changes to the nation’s voter roll, many leaders of the strongman’s own governing coalition were alarmed, as Mr. Modi maintained his trademark silence on anything negative.

But how Mr. Modi has dealt with the unrest in recent days — locking down the heart of New Delhi, detaining protest leaders and rounding up protesters by the thousands — signaled a better prepared strategy that has reassured some of his backers that he can stall the momentum of the protest movement, according to interviews with more than half a dozen senior members of the governing coalition. Most of them asked not be identified as they are not authorized to publicly discuss internal strategy.

The government’s approach is two-pronged, they said.

First: Quash any mobilizing effort that suggests that public anger is the continuation of the organic Gen Z eruption over the summer that, by all accounts, unsettled Mr. Modi’s grip on power.

Second: Allow the gatherings of the traditional opposition parties to go ahead, framing the fight squarely against a traditional foe that Mr. Modi has repeatedly beaten at elections and is confident of vanquishing again.

For now, the approach appears to be working.

The “cockroach” youth movement — which began this summer over the failings of the education system and was revived this autumn over accusations that Mr. Modi is manipulating India’s election system — has become bogged down by the enormous powers of the state thrown at them.

Their momentum has deflated as their leaders move in and out of detention, and get tangled up in legal cases that could follow them for years. Security forces have met protest calls by putting locations under lockdown and flooding the area with uniformed officers. Organizers and supporters are stopped at the city gates, pulled out of trains and buses, and in many cases held in their homes or barricaded inside their university campuses.

Broadcast media seen as friendly to the government has then declared the low turnout a flop.

The organized political opposition, on the other hand, has received a boost from the rare public challenge to Mr. Modi. But the anti-Modi coalition has long been a fragile one, its unity frequently tested by internal competition on local turf across the country.

Mr. Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party has long portrayed the strongman as less of a prime minister of a coalition government, and more of an executive ruler. It is framing the current agitation as an effort by Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition bloc, to topple Mr. Modi through violent means.

“Their intention is pure and simple regime change,” Smriti Irani, a senior B.J.P. leader and former cabinet minister who defeated Mr. Gandhi in his constituency in 2019, said in TV appearances last week. “An unelectable prince, who hopes to be emperor one day, is now throwing a political tantrum.”

Still, Mr. Modi has found himself in troubled waters that he has not experienced in his 12 years at the national helm, many of the governing coalition leaders said. A nonpartisan civil society is managing to break through and question government failures in ways that the B.J.P. cannot easily dismiss as old-school partisan politics.

There was already some discontent within Mr. Modi’s camp before the protest movement. Some figures within the B.J.P. and other parties in his coalition had become disgruntled by how much power has become centralized.

“The opposition is not a problem for them,” said Durga Nand Jha, an academic who leads a think tank affiliated with the B.J.P.’s parent organization. “The problem is, why is the public and their own supporters not defending them? They are struggling to consolidate their own supporters in this moment — some are opposing, some are silent, some are just sitting at home.”

The B.J.P. has become overly dependent on state levers and electoral machinations at the cost of political dynamism, according to party leaders and analysts. In several states, supporters have been disheartened over what they see as a heavily top-down approach to local elections and issues.

Party leaders, however, expressed confidence that they would still be better placed than the opposition Congress Party, which is struggling to translate the growing popularity of its leader, Mr. Gandhi, to an actual revival of its cadres at the local and state levels.

“A few thousand protesters here and there — students, farmers, businessmen — don’t make a dent in our winnibility,” said Krishna Kant Shukla, a B.J.P. leader in Uttar Pradesh, India’s largest state of 240 million people, which will hold an election next year.

The summer youth protests had drawn large crowds, including many youth from families not associated with the opposition, according to one B.J.P. leader and two leaders of parties in the ruling coalition. The youth were irreverent in how they poked fun at Mr. Modi with their placards and memes. Many, on camera, suggested they came from families who supported the ruling party.

The task of handling political agitation falls to Amit Shah, Mr. Modi’s powerful home minister, who is his effective No. 2 and has been at his side for over two decades.

Ahead of the protests this month in New Delhi, Mr. Shah deployed tens of thousands of security forces and barricaded a large swath of the city center to make sure crowds similar to those from the summer could not gather.

But even during the crackdown, there was an interesting let up: The police allowed a large gathering of the Congress Party and its opposition alliance partners to crowd into central Delhi. Mr. Modi’s supporters then cast the gathering as Mr. Gandhi attempting a power grab — choosing a preferred foe to address rather than acknowledging that it was facing a problem with youth anger.

Behind the bravado, Mr. Modi’s party is facing the moment on shakier ground.

After losing his party’s parliamentary majority in 2024, Mr. Modi has been dependent on several coalition partners.

How he holds together his alliance will be key, particularly if the youth movement grows and his partners see their ties with the ruling party as a liability.

Leaders from two parties that have brought support to Mr. Modi complained that Mr. Modi and Mr. Shah rarely consult leaders of their own B.J.P., let alone those from coalition partners. A leader from one of the allied parties likened Mr. Modi to Indira Gandhi, the prime minister who suspended democracy for two years in the 1970s. Neither could take criticism, the party leader said.

As the youth movement has faced the brunt of the state’s suppression, its leaders have been questioned for not coordinating more closely with the organized opposition to find safety in numbers.

But Anish Gawande, a spokesman for an opposition party who also maintains close ties to leaders of the youth movement, said that such merging would play right into Mr. Modi’s designs.

“It’s only if the third space opens up that the opposition can revive itself,” Mr. Gawande said.

He said the youth movement needed to reinvent itself in the face of government suppression, but the harsh crackdown was helping with the movement’s broader mission for accountability: by exposing the repressive measures of Mr. Modi’s government. Its heavy-handedness, particularly the repeated detention of youth leaders for nonviolent marches, may backfire with a younger generation.

“You have to realize that you cannot constantly do this, that these security forces cannot sit in Delhi for the next year,” Mr. Gawande said. “So just as the state tires us out, we also tire the state out.”

item.title: Shark Returns to Sea After Over a Month Stuck in a South Korean Port Canal
item.description:
A 10-foot-long shark that became a celebrity in South Korea after being trapped in a canal in the southeastern city of Busan for more than a month has returned to the open ocean.

Local officials on Wednesday successfully guided the dusky shark, nicknamed “Bukangi,” who had been stuck in the waterway at one of the country’s busiest ports, back into open water, according to a local news network’s livestream of the effort. Rescuers attached a wide net to a floating device, which they pulled across the canal using ropes. As the net swept across the water, guiding the shark out, divers made sure it did not get tangled on the canal bed. The process took several hours.

Hundreds of people gathered to watch, with crowds lining both sides of the canal and inching forward as rescuers dragged the net. More tuned in online. “Come back again!” said one online commenter after Bukangi was freed.

The rescue on Wednesday followed two failed attempts. The authorities first tried to guide the shark out of the canal on Sept. 29 using boats and water pumps, but Bukangi dove too far below the surface. The second attempt, on Oct. 2, failed because the rescuers’ net got tangled on the canal bed and the shark managed to swim over it.

The Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and the Busan local government were among several agencies that worked on Wednesday’s rescue mission.

Bukangi, who was named by South Koreans after the Bukhang Waterfront Park, where she was trapped, is over 20 years old, experts say. She is the first wild shark to appear in the canal and has become a sensation in South Korea since being first spotted on Sept. 18. Researchers said they were worried because she had not been feeding and would not survive the colder water temperatures in November. Dusky sharks, which live in temperate to tropical waters, can survive up to a month without food.

Over a million people from around the country visited the park to catch a glimpse of the apex predator. The local government has made her an honorary city ambassador.

item.title: As Alberta Rejects Separatism, Carney Gets Much of the Credit
item.description:
For Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada, the decision by oil-rich Alberta to ask voters whether to remain in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on secession came, as he put it last week, “at the worst possible time.”

But timing aside, Monday’s resounding vote to keep the western province within Canada both strengthens national unity and eliminates a significant distraction as Mr. Carney works to form new global alliances in the face of the trade and diplomatic war that President Trump has waged against Canada since he returned to office.

After months of campaigning, 75.2 percent of Albertans voted to remain in Canada, while 24.8 percent favored holding a second, binding vote on separation, according to unofficial results.

Neither Mr. Carney nor his Liberal government had a formal role in the referendum, which was called by Danielle Smith, Alberta’s conservative premier. But many analysts attributed the strong vote for Canada to policies Mr. Carney, who was raised in the province, introduced over the past year and to his campaigning for continued unity here.

“Carney was huge,” said Duane Bratt, a professor at Mount Royal University in Calgary, Alberta, who studies Alberta politics. “His working with Smith really took the wind out of separatism, and that’s why the separatists were just flailing.”

He added, “Mark Carney is the most popular politician in the province right now.”

Even after accounting for Mr. Carney’s upbringing in Edmonton, for a Liberal prime minister to enjoy outsize popularity is an anomaly in Alberta, the home of Canadian conservatism, where Conservative candidates frequently win federal elections in landslides.

Even today, many Albertans still complain about a government policy almost 50 years ago under the Liberal prime minister Pierre Elliot Trudeau. His short-lived National Energy Program of 1980, which sought to lower the Canadian price for oil, was popular elsewhere in Canada. But it was deeply resented in Alberta, where it was widely seen as an intrusion on the provinces’ control over natural resources.

When Mr. Carney, former governor of the central banks of Canada and of England, entered politics last year, Ms. Smith seized every opportunity to criticize what she called the federal government’s “nine bad laws,” environmental measures introduced by his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, Pierre’s son. She also relentlessly pushed for a second oil pipeline to the Pacific Coast from her landlocked province.

Since then, Mr. Carney has replaced most of the “nine bad laws” with what he calls “cooperative federalism.” The new approach includes a new system that he said would speed up environmental and regulatory approvals of large projects, including oil and gas developments. More significantly, he said the federal government would build and largely finance an oil pipeline to a new ship terminal near Vancouver, British Columbia, the province just west of Alberta.

While Mr. Carney’s changes were condemned by some environmentalists and Indigenous communities, they undercut separatist claims that Canada holds Alberta back from its full economic potential.

As a result, Mr. Bratt said, separatist campaigners were reduced to saying that Mr. Carney “was going to cancel the pipeline the day after the referendum or ask why he wasn’t building it personally by hand — just all sorts of crazy stuff.”

Polls show that Albertans support Mr. Carney’s defiant approach to Mr. Trump, as do Canadians generally. Ms. Smith, by contrast, who became leader of the United Conservative Party and then premier largely with the support of separatists, has frequently urged caution and restraint in dealing with Washington.

She initially joined other provinces’ leaders in banning the sale of American beer, wine and spirits from the provincial liquor distribution system to pressure the Trump administration. But she soon allowed the products’ return, leaving Alberta as the only province without any measures against American alcohol.

Ms. Smith and Mr. Carney also contrasted during the referendum campaign. After a court quashed separatist efforts to force a direct question on leaving through a petition, Ms. Smith changed the law to add the separatism question to a previously planned referendum. She then alienated separatists by saying that she would vote for Canada; she did not require her party’s elected members to follow suit. Her own campaigning for Canada was limited, and she often focused on reasons for leaving the country.

Although Mr. Carney acknowledged that Albertans have causes for complaint and that Canada “isn’t perfect,” he vigorously pushed back against the separatist movement and the referendum. His message was well received. About 7,000 people lined up last week in Calgary, the province’s largest city — some for up to two hours — for a rally where he was the headliner.

On Tuesday, Mr. Carney made no attempt to hide his delight as he headed into a cabinet meeting in Ottawa.

“It’s a great result for Canada, thrilled that Albertans have chosen unity,” he told reporters, adding in French: “It’s a good day for Canada.”

item.title: When Starshield Cut Out, Ukrainian Drones Fell From the Skies
item.description:
A senior Ukrainian commander said he had dozens of armed drones soaring toward Russian military targets last week when, all at once, the video feeds streaming their flight paths went fuzzy.

The drones had lost their connection to pilots on the ground through Starshield, a Pentagon-funded satellite internet service, said the commander, Oleh, who spoke on the condition that he be identified by only his first name to protect operational security. Many of the drones simply fell from the sky, he said: The effect cost his units more than $1 million worth of weaponry.

The Starshield disruptions forced Oleh to halt almost all operations for the next three days, he said, including strikes on Russian command posts and fuel hubs. Such attacks, he said, help save the lives of Ukrainian troops holding positions on the front and slow Russian advances.

Ukrainian accounts of Starshield’s abrupt throttling have become a flashpoint in a worsening feud between President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine and President Trump. A week after the first problems were reported, Ukrainian troops said that the situation had improved but that connectivity issues remained. The Trump administration has offered mixed messages, both denying any change to Starshield service and saying that service has been restored.

Ukrainian officials fear that the Trump administration ordered the disruptions to punish Ukraine over its strikes on Russian oil refineries and to force Kyiv to capitulate in the war. Ukraine has also reported gaps in the sharing of U.S. military intelligence and delays in the delivery of American interceptor missiles. U.S. officials deny any such disruptions.

Starshield is a military-grade sister system to Elon Musk’s Starlink, and European countries pay for Ukraine’s access to it. The more advanced Starshield system is not available to all Ukrainian troops, but many rely on it to fly drones and use standard Starlink connections for more basic communications. Ukrainian officials have reported slowdowns with both Starshield and Starlink.

Mr. Musk has said that Starshield is controlled by the Pentagon. Secretary of State Marco Rubio added to the confusion on Wednesday when he asserted that it was Mr. Musk’s company, SpaceX, that determined access to Starlink and Starshield.

The initial Starshield throttling caused Ukrainian drones to lose their connection to the system when flying at speeds as low as 40 miles an hour, Ukrainian officials said. Connectivity has since improved, Ukrainian officials say, but drones still lose their connection when they exceed 100 m.p.h. Some models can operate normally under that speed, but others, including those used by Oleh’s troops, must fly faster to strike.

The speed limits have also thwarted interceptors used to take down Russian drones that attack Ukrainian cities, Mr. Zelensky said. Fearing that the systems may never be fully restored or could cut off abruptly again, Ukraine is searching for workarounds, a scramble that commanders say is diverting soldiers’ attention from the battlefield.

Ukrainian officials say they are seeking answers about who ordered the slowdowns of Starshield and Starlink — and why.

Asked for comment, a White House official said in a statement that there had been no changes to satellite internet in Ukraine. On Friday, Mr. Trump said that any change “wasn’t me” and that “from what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.” Mr. Rubio said a day later that a Starlink slowdown in Ukraine had “sort of happened” but added that “my understanding is it’s been restored.”

Mr. Zelensky has called the changes to Starshield “a planned operation.” On the NBC show “Meet the Press” on Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that “President Trump and Secretary Rubio have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that, and I think it is very reckless for President Zelensky to make such a charge.”

In Washington, politicians from both parties called on Mr. Trump to restore Ukraine’s satellite connectivity.

After a group of lawmakers spoke by video call with Mr. Zelensky on Monday, Senator Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina, said that the Ukrainian leader “confirmed ongoing Starlink disruptions, reported interruptions to critical U.S. intelligence sharing and raised concerns about delays in air-defense interceptors.”

“Degrading Ukraine’s satellite communications, weakening its air defenses and easing sanctions against Russia only embolden Putin and prolong this war,” Mr. Tillis said, referring to a move by Mr. Trump to allow the United States to buy Russian diesel fuel.

On Tuesday, Mr. Zelensky said he and Mr. Rubio had a “substantive discussion” about Starshield, as well as about shortages of missile interceptors and recent disruptions to early warning systems about Russian ballistic missile attacks.

Any claim that the United States held back on warnings for Ukraine is “simply not accurate,” Mr. Rubio said after his call with Mr. Zelensky. He also noted that Patriot interceptors were in short supply around the world. “Nothing is being deliberately denied to Ukraine,” he said.

While the American political machinations over Starshield remained murky, Ukrainian commanders said the effects of restrictions on the system were clear on the battlefield.

Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky, who recently assumed command of thousands of troops of the Center Grouping of Forces in eastern Ukraine, said troops were adapting to the new speed limits.

Before now, Ukrainian drones using Starshield flew as fast as 250 miles an hour with a stable connection, he said. The formal limit had already been 100 m.p.h., but it had not been enforced, General Biletsky said.

That leaves open the possibility that the United States could assert that no change had occurred in the system even as Ukraine experienced changes on the front.

Even if Ukraine can adapt to allow its attack drones to work under the limits, General Biletsky said, interceptors that used Starshield to counter Russian jet-powered drones would still be hindered. The only way to take down an incoming drone is to outrace it, and jet-powered Russian weapons fly far faster than 100 m.p.h.

Reducing the speed limits for air defense “is a painful decision that literally undermines the protection of our cities, first and foremost,” General Biletsky said. “So when the Pentagon took this step, it was undoubtedly an unfriendly move toward Ukraine’s civilian population.”

In command posts across Ukraine, there was little doubt that the Starshield restrictions were the result of a political decision, not a technical glitch. Ukrainian troops had long feared that Washington would pressure Kyiv into concessions by cutting off satellite connections.

As Oleh’s drones fell last week, his three phones buzzed with expletive-laden calls from stunned troops, who rushed to redirect and save as much of their gear as they could.

Oleh recalled soldiers telling him that they felt abandoned. He said that it was well past time for Ukraine to take off its rose-colored glasses and stop seeing the United States as an ally.

Lt. Yuriy Butusov, company commander of the 23rd Assault Regiment in Ukraine’s Khartia Corps, said his troops had been hamstrung by the slowed connections, which essentially gave the Russian military “a vacation day.”

“This day without Starlink saved many lives and many trucks for Russia, unfortunately,” Lieutenant Butusov said.

“It’s a big cost for us,” he added. “And much more blood. Our blood.”
